sections.title: Opening pages
sections.html:
Mastering General Lines Property and Casualty

A complete post licensing guide and 16 week practice curriculum for Texas insurance professionals

Prepared for Sunday Pastores | September 2026

This handbook teaches the working judgment behind personal and commercial P&C insurance: exposure discovery, policy interpretation, underwriting, claims triage, Texas requirements, and client communication. Chapters 1 through 23 form the reference guide. The workbook that follows turns each topic into a 16 week course with cases, drills, and a capstone. Use current issued forms and official sources for actual transactions.

Scope. Examples are educational and simplified. Carrier contracts, endorsements, current rules, and individual facts control real coverage. For a disputed claim or legal question, consult the insurer and qualified counsel.

Working rule. Every coverage answer must identify the exact issued or proposed form, edition, declarations, endorsements, exclusions, conditions, limits, deductible, facts, and date. These exercises use fictional facts and illustrative wording. Do not treat an exercise answer as a coverage determination.

sections.title: Chapters
sections.html:
Chapters

Part I Foundations of Real World Property and Casualty

Chapter 1 The Insurance Contract

An insurance contract is a promise tied to defined facts and conditions. A producer should begin with the issued policy, not a marketing summary. Confirm the named insured, policy period, property or autos scheduled, coverage limits, deductible, and form edition on the declarations. Then read the insuring agreement to identify the event that triggers the insurer's promise. A liability insuring agreement may turn on an occurrence and bodily injury during the policy period; a property agreement may turn on direct physical loss by a covered cause. An apparently similar event can fall under different coverage parts.

Definitions change ordinary language. A person living in a household may or may not fit a policy's defined insured; a building, detached structure, tenant improvement, and movable equipment can occupy different categories. Exclusions remove specific risks, but an exception can restore a narrower part. Conditions govern notice, cooperation, proof of loss, preservation of property, or other duties. Endorsements amend the base form and can replace a clause entirely. Read their effective dates and precedence carefully.

To identify a gap, compare the client's exposure map with the entire set of actual policy grants. For each exposure, record the form, applicable limit and deductible, major exclusion or sublimit, and open question. Do not call an uncovered exposure an exclusion when it simply never met the insuring agreement. When uncertain, ask underwriting or coverage counsel through the agency's process and describe uncertainty to the client without promising an outcome.

Field exercise. Analyze a proposal that lists a $500,000 liability limit but omits the applicable form and endorsements. List five facts you must obtain before saying what that limit protects.

sections.title: Chapter 2 Risk Perils and Hazards
sections.html:
Chapter 2 Risk Perils and Hazards

Risk is the possibility of loss; a peril is a cause of loss such as fire, theft, or hail; a hazard increases either the likelihood or severity of a loss. A worn electrical panel is a physical hazard. An applicant's deliberate misstatement is a moral hazard. Carelessness that arises because the insured assumes someone else will pay is sometimes described as a morale hazard. Treat these as analytical concepts, not labels to apply to people casually.

A direct loss damages covered property; an indirect loss may follow from it, such as lost income during repairs. A property policy may cover the first and require a separate business income provision for the second. Underwriters evaluate frequency, severity, location, construction, occupancy, protection, management, loss history, and risk controls. One carrier may decline a risk under its current appetite while another accepts it with a different deductible, exclusion, or price.

Build a risk narrative rather than manipulating a rating field. A restaurant with a hood suppression system, cleaning logs, and trained staff presents different evidence from one with unknown maintenance. Explain the operation truthfully and provide photographs, inspections, and loss runs when requested. Declination is a placement decision, not proof that coverage is impossible in every market.

Field exercise. Write a four-column hazard table for a rental house with old wiring, occasional vacancy, and a short term rental plan.

sections.title: Part II Personal Lines Mastery
sections.html:
Part II Personal Lines Mastery

Chapter 3 Homeowners Insurance HO 1 Through HO 8

The HO labels describe families of standardized forms, but Texas insurers can use approved company-specific contracts. HO 1 and HO 2 are more limited named-peril designs; HO 3 commonly uses broader building coverage with named-peril personal property; HO 4 is designed for renters; HO 5 is broader in common standardized designs; HO 6 serves condominium unit owners; and HO 8 is adapted to certain older homes. This shorthand is a starting point only. Never infer coverage solely from the label.

The typical coverage map is A dwelling, B other structures, C personal property, D loss of use, E personal liability, and F medical payments to others. Compare percentage-based limits to actual need. A policy might show a large dwelling limit but only a small jewelry theft sublimit. An unattached garage, home business stock, or rented accessory dwelling may require a separate review. Explain whether property is settled at replacement cost or actual cash value and whether replacement cost is paid only after actual repair or replacement.

In Texas, wind and hail deductibles may be expressed as a percentage of dwelling coverage. On a $400,000 Coverage A limit, a 2 percent deductible is $8,000, not 2 percent of the claim. Flood is generally separate. Coastal wind and hail may also need a separate placement. Discuss water backup, foundation, seepage, equipment breakdown, service line, roof settlement, ordinance or law, and scheduled valuable articles with the current form in hand.

Claim example: a hailstorm damages a roof while a plumbing leak has stained an upstairs ceiling. Two events call for separate dates, causes, deductibles, and policy clauses. Photographs and contractor estimates are useful, but the insurer determines covered scope and depreciation. Document what is known and avoid merging the events into one claim narrative.

Field exercise. Compare two home proposals with equal premium but different roof settlement and wind deductible terms. Write the client explanation.

sections.title: Chapter 4 Dwelling Policies DP 1 DP 2 DP 3
sections.html:
Chapter 4 Dwelling Policies DP 1 DP 2 DP 3

A dwelling policy often serves a house that does not fit an owner-occupied homeowners program, including a long-term rental or certain vacant properties. DP 1, DP 2, and DP 3 commonly reflect different covered-peril approaches, but carrier forms and endorsements decide the actual protection. A dwelling policy may have no personal liability unless added or purchased separately. Tenant belongings generally belong on the tenant's own renters policy.

Record ownership entity, occupancy, lease terms, length of vacancy, renovation work, property manager, and whether the home is used for short-term stays. Vacancy and unoccupancy are not interchangeable; read the form's definitions and vacancy conditions. A house between tenants for two weeks differs from one stripped for a six-month remodel. A landlord's loss of rental income coverage also has its own trigger and limits.

Valuation needs particular attention. An older rental with a replacement estimate above market value can still require adequate insured value if the policy uses replacement cost and coinsurance. Actual cash value can leave a substantial repair gap. DP forms may treat theft, vandalism, water, and wind differently. Ask for the full form, not merely the declarations.

Field exercise. A landlord changes a long-term rental to weekend stays. Draft the questions and carrier referral before any coverage assurance.

sections.title: Chapter 5 Personal Auto Insurance
sections.html:
Chapter 5 Personal Auto Insurance

Texas's current liability minimum is 30/60/25: $30,000 bodily injury per person, $60,000 bodily injury per accident, and $25,000 property damage per accident. These are legal minimums, not a recommended risk limit. A multi-car crash or serious injury can exceed them quickly. Quote higher limits when appropriate and record the client's choice.

Liability pays for covered injury or property damage owed to others, subject to the policy. Physical damage protects the insured vehicle through collision and other-than-collision coverage, subject to deductible and valuation. Personal injury protection and uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage must be offered in Texas, with written rejection if the client declines. Medical payments is a different coverage. Read the actual forms for eligible people, stacking, offsets, exclusions, and claim coordination.

Household drivers, garaging, permissive users, delivery work, rideshare, business use, rental cars, trailers, custom equipment, and newly acquired vehicles create underwriting and coverage questions. Rental reimbursement and roadside assistance have separate triggers and dollar or day limits. A loan payoff can exceed an actual cash value settlement; discuss loan or lease gap coverage where available.

Claim example: an adult child living at home borrows a listed vehicle and collides during app-based delivery. Do not decide coverage from the word 'permissive.' Find the driver disclosure, vehicle, app stage, commercial-use exclusion, any endorsement, and platform policy. Notify the insurer promptly with complete facts.

Field exercise. Explain the difference between 30/60/25 and 100/300/100 using a two-injury accident and a $45,000 property damage demand.

sections.title: Chapter 6 Umbrella and Excess Liability
sections.html:
Chapter 6 Umbrella and Excess Liability

An excess policy adds limit above specified underlying coverage. An umbrella may also have its own coverage language, potentially broader in limited circumstances, but 'drop down' is never automatic. An umbrella can require particular underlying policies and limits, a retained limit for certain uncovered-by-primary exposures, and scheduled vehicles or properties. Its exclusions may differ from the primary policy.

Start with a household inventory: homes, rentals, vehicles, boats, drivers, dogs, pools, volunteer activity, and business interests. Compare the primary and umbrella definitions of insured, covered activity, territorial reach, and defense. A client with a rental property omitted from the umbrella schedule could face a different response than expected. An auto policy at lower limits than the umbrella requires can leave a gap the client pays.

Explain the role of the umbrella without promising every lawsuit is covered. Confirm underlying limits at inception and each renewal, especially after a carrier change.

Field exercise. A client adds a rental and replaces an auto carrier midyear. List the umbrella checks and file notes.

sections.title: Part III Commercial Lines Mastery
sections.html:
Part III Commercial Lines Mastery

Chapter 7 Commercial Property

Commercial property separates buildings, business personal property, and property of others. Tenant improvements, outdoor signs, stock, mobile equipment, and tools away from the premises may require special treatment. Read covered causes of loss and endorsements; the label 'special' does not mean every cause is covered.

Business income covers defined income loss after a qualifying physical damage event, subject to period of restoration, waiting period, limit or coinsurance, and exclusions. Extra expense can pay certain costs to reduce suspension or continue operations. The client should preserve profit and loss statements, sales records, payroll, leases, purchase orders, and repair timelines. A utility outage without damage at the scheduled premises may require a utility services endorsement and its own trigger.

Coinsurance is a valuation condition. If a building's insurable value is $1 million and an 80 percent clause applies, $800,000 is the illustrative amount to carry to satisfy it; a lesser amount can reduce partial loss payment. Apply the form's precise calculation and deductible. Ordinance or law can address code-driven demolition, increased construction cost, and undamaged portions after a covered loss. Inland marine often addresses mobile property or property in transit.

Fire case: a café's kitchen burns, closing it for eight weeks. Separate damaged equipment and tenant improvements from lost net income, continuing expenses, extra expense, spoiled inventory, and any code upgrades. Each item needs its own form and evidence.

Field exercise. Create an eight-column schedule of property, location, value, form, cause, deductible, sublimit, and unresolved question.

sections.title: Chapter 8 Commercial General Liability
sections.html:
Chapter 8 Commercial General Liability

The CGL commonly has Coverage A for bodily injury and property damage, Coverage B for personal and advertising injury, and Coverage C for medical payments. Coverage A often requires bodily injury or property damage caused by an occurrence in the coverage territory and period. Read the aggregate, products and completed operations aggregate, each occurrence limit, exclusions, definitions, and defense provision.

Do not assume a CGL pays to repair the insured's own defective work. A contractor's bad installation, damage to other property, and injury to a third party pose different questions under different exclusions and exceptions. Completed operations can be important after work is finished. Certificates summarize reported coverage but do not amend a policy. Additional insured status depends on an actual endorsement and its wording, often restricted by operations, contract, or timing.

Most standard CGL forms are occurrence based. Claims-made structures are common in some professional and specialty liability products and depend on reporting dates and retroactive dates. A contract's demand for 'additional insured' or 'primary and noncontributory' should be translated into actual carrier-approved endorsements; never certify language that has not been issued.

Contractor case: a railing installed last year fails this year. Document the project, contract, date of work, date of injury, alleged cause, named insured, subcontractors, policies in both years, and endorsements. Submit without determining the insurer's defense obligation yourself.

Field exercise. Mark the exact clause path for a slip-and-fall at a client's leased office and list three facts still needed.

sections.title: Chapter 9 Businessowners Policy
sections.html:
Chapter 9 Businessowners Policy

A businessowners policy packages property and liability for eligible businesses, often with business income and other built-in or optional features. Eligibility depends on carrier appetite, class, building size, revenue, operations, location, and loss history. A convenient package is not automatically broader than separate commercial policies.

A commercial package policy assembles selected coverage parts and common conditions; it is often more configurable for larger or unusual risks. Compare limits, sublimits, exclusions, business income terms, cyber features, equipment breakdown, and property off premises. A café may fit one carrier's BOP while a restaurant with late-night alcohol service or delivery may not.

The reason small businesses favor a BOP is often simpler placement and administration, but the producer's job is to test whether it fits the exposure. Confirm property ownership, tenant improvements, inventory peaks, employee counts, vehicles, contracts, and online activity before recommending it.

Field exercise. Compare a BOP proposal and separate property plus CGL proposals for the café case.

sections.title: Chapter 10 Commercial Auto
sections.html:
Chapter 10 Commercial Auto

Commercial auto symbols determine which autos apply to each coverage. In common business auto forms, symbol 1 means any auto, 2 owned autos only, 7 specifically described autos, 8 hired autos only, and 9 nonowned autos only; symbols 3 through 6 address narrower owned categories. Read each coverage's symbol on the declarations. A symbol for liability does not imply the same symbol for physical damage.

Hired autos generally involve vehicles the business leases, hires, rents, or borrows under the form's definitions; nonowned autos often include employees' vehicles used in company business. Ask who owns, drives, dispatches, and maintains each vehicle. Personal policies may exclude or restrict certain business activity. Some trucking operations have federal financial responsibility obligations. MCS-90 is a federal public liability endorsement for qualifying motor carriers, not a substitute for a suitable commercial auto program or cargo coverage.

Trucking claim: a driver uses an unscheduled borrowed truck to haul customer goods and injures a motorist. Separate public liability, damage to the truck, cargo loss, hired auto status, driver eligibility, and federal filing obligations. Refer federal and interstate issues to the carrier's transportation specialist.

Field exercise. Read a commercial auto declarations page and mark liability and physical damage symbols separately.

sections.title: Chapter 11 Workers Compensation and Employers Liability
sections.html:
Chapter 11 Workers Compensation and Employers Liability

Most Texas private employers can choose whether to carry workers compensation, although exceptions and contract requirements matter. A subscribing employer's workers compensation policy supplies statutory benefits for covered employee work injuries. Employers liability addresses certain employer legal liability exposures outside the benefits part, subject to terms and limits. A nonsubscriber faces a different legal and insurance landscape, and alternative benefit arrangements should be reviewed by qualified advisers.

Do not call a worker a subcontractor merely because the applicant issues a 1099. Gather who directs the work, controls equipment, hires helpers, and pays wages, then refer classification questions to the carrier and counsel. Payroll, job class, state of work, and experience history affect premium. Audits can change the final premium if estimated exposure differs from actual exposure.

A worker falls at a contractor's jobsite while employed by a subcontractor. Preserve contracts, certificates, payroll and assignment facts; notify potentially involved insurers. Avoid deciding employer status, compensability, or exclusive-remedy issues for the client.

Field exercise. Compare a subscribing and nonsubscribing Texas employer's questions about employee injuries and required filings.

sections.title: Chapter 12 Professional Liability and Specialty Lines
sections.html:
Chapter 12 Professional Liability and Specialty Lines

CGL is primarily designed around specified bodily injury, property damage, and personal and advertising injury. A professional mistake causing purely financial loss may need errors and omissions insurance. Directors and officers coverage addresses certain management claims, employment practices liability addresses specified workplace allegations, and cyber coverage can include breach response, business interruption, and liability components. None is interchangeable.

Claims-made policies require precise attention to retroactive date, policy period, reporting window, prior and pending matters, continuity, and the definition of claim. A cheaper renewal can create a serious gap if the retroactive date resets. Cyber policies vary in the services they supply, panel requirements, exclusions, waiting periods, and sublimits.

A stolen laptop at a bookkeeping firm may involve notification expenses, forensic investigation, contractual demands, and privacy claims. First establish facts and contact the insurer's prescribed response channel. Do not hire a vendor or admit legal liability on behalf of the insurer without authorization.

Field exercise. Build an exposure-to-policy map for a real estate brokerage with staff, customer data, vehicles, and professional advice.

sections.title: Part IV Texas Specific Knowledge
sections.html:
Part IV Texas Specific Knowledge

Chapter 13 Texas Department of Insurance Rules

A Texas producer should keep the licensing file as carefully as the sales file. TDI currently lists 24 CE hours every two years for General Lines P&C, including three hours of ethics. Confirm your own renewal date and transcript. TDI says appointments must be filed before agent transactions. A license does not itself give an agent authority to bind for a carrier; check contracts and written procedures.

Prohibited-practices questions can arise in rebates, gifts, referral arrangements, advertising, and representations of coverage. Do not improvise a legal rule from a brief online summary. Route a proposed promotion through agency compliance and current Texas law. Keep quote versions, client requests, written rejections, effective dates, and proof of any required delivery.

Texas auto liability minimums are 30/60/25. PIP and UM/UIM are offered subject to written rejection requirements. The consumer rights materials should be part of the agent's working reference. For coastal risks, do not assume a homeowners policy covers wind and hail or flood; verify forms, eligibility, and separate effective dates.

Field exercise. Audit a fictional file missing a written UM/UIM decision, carrier appointment confirmation, and a recorded roof deductible discussion.

sections.title: Chapter 14 Texas Claims Handling
sections.html:
Chapter 14 Texas Claims Handling

The agent's role is to listen, document, help deliver notice, explain the process, and follow up. The adjuster investigates facts and applies the policy on the insurer's behalf. Prompt payment and claim handling rules impose deadlines on insurers, but the clock and exceptions depend on the type of claim, information received, and any catastrophe extension. Use TDI's current claim guidance for a live matter.

A claim can involve inspection, cause analysis, valuation, deductible, depreciation, proof of loss, defense, settlement, subrogation, and salvage. Replacement cost may be paid in stages, with recoverable depreciation after completed repair under the policy. Subrogation concerns recovery from a responsible third party after payment. Bad faith and statutory extra-contractual liability are legal issues for counsel, not a producer's casual conclusion.

Texas case example for research, not a blanket rule: USAA Texas Lloyds Co. v. Menchaca, 545 S.W.3d 479 (Tex. 2018), addresses the relationship between policy benefits and statutory claims. Another case can turn on distinct facts and later law. For a disputed claim, preserve the denial letter, policy, communications, estimates, and timeline, then refer the client to the insurer's review process and appropriate professional advice.

Field exercise. Draft a neutral update after a disputed roof inspection, identifying what the carrier decided and what is still being reviewed.

sections.title: Part V Underwriting and Agency Operations
sections.html:
Part V Underwriting and Agency Operations

Chapter 15 Carrier Underwriting Logic

An appetite guide describes the classes, locations, construction, protection, loss history, limits, and operations a carrier prefers or will not write. It is not the policy. Underwriting assesses expected frequency and severity along with uncertainty and controls. A risk can move from acceptable to referral when roof age, vacancy, wildfire or hail exposure, prior losses, or a change in operation is discovered.

A useful submission explains the risk as it exists. Include year built, updates, inspections, photographs, entity and ownership, payroll or sales, loss runs, safety practices, and the desired coverage structure. Say what is unknown. Do not change an answer solely to receive a quote. If a risk is declined, ask which criterion drove the result and whether remediation, a different market, a higher deductible, or a specialty product is appropriate.

Deductible strategy should account for the client's cash available after loss. A percentage deductible may materially reduce premium while transferring thousands of dollars of risk. Document the dollar illustration and client acceptance.

Field exercise. Explain an underwriter's likely questions about a vacant rental with two water claims and an older roof.

sections.title: Chapter 16 Agency Workflow
sections.html:
Chapter 16 Agency Workflow

A sound agency workflow moves from consent and discovery to application, quote, form review, recommendation, written selection, binding confirmation, delivery, service, claim support, and renewal. The CRM or agency management system should preserve source documents and dates, not just a premium figure. Set tasks for carrier referrals, inspections, payment, lender evidence, and expiration.

Quoting multiple carriers requires equal exposure data and a coverage comparison. If one quote changes limits, roof terms, property valuation, water coverage, or business income, make the difference prominent. A producer may request a binder only within delegated authority and required conditions. An endorsement request is not completed until the carrier accepts and issues it. A certificate of insurance conveys information; it cannot extend coverage or create additional insured status on its own.

Renewal begins before the last week. Review changes in buildings, autos, drivers, employees, revenue, contracts, claims, and carrier forms. Maintain a change log comparing expiring and renewal terms. For a material reduction, document the client's notice and decision.

Field exercise. Design a 90-day renewal checklist with owners, deadlines, evidence and escalation points.

sections.title: Chapter 17 Sales Ethics and Client Management
sections.html:
Chapter 17 Sales Ethics and Client Management

An ethical sale starts with discovery. Ask what the client owns, who can be injured, what income would stop, what contracts require, and how much loss the client can absorb. Present options in plain language: premium, limits, deductibles, valuation, exclusions, and unresolved underwriting conditions. A low price is meaningful only after those differences are visible.

Professional liability risk grows when an agent promises 'full coverage,' assumes a policy was bound, leaves a recommendation undocumented, or uses a certificate to satisfy a contract without an endorsement. Record the request, advice, options, client choice, insurer response, effective date, and follow up. Do not hide a coverage gap simply because a client resists the premium.

When a client is upset after a claim or renewal increase, distinguish empathy from admission. A useful response acknowledges the concern, states the confirmed facts, identifies the insurer decision maker, and commits to a specific follow up time. Never alter the historical file after a dispute without an accurate dated correction.

Field exercise. Write a 200-word explanation to a client who wants the cheapest home policy despite a roof ACV endorsement.

sections.title: Part VI Scenarios and Case Studies
sections.html:
Part VI Scenarios and Case Studies

Chapter 18 Personal Lines Scenarios

Dog bite: identify whose dog, where the bite happened, whether the injured person is an insured, the underlying liability form, animal exclusions, prior incidents, and any umbrella condition. Notify the carrier; do not promise defense. Fire loss: separate dwelling, other structures, personal property, loss of use, debris removal, ordinance or law, mortgagee interest, deductible, and proof of ownership. Preserve photographs and receipts.

Water damage: establish source and timeline. A burst supply line, long-term seepage, sewer backup, and rising surface water are distinct mechanisms. Read water exclusions and endorsements before responding. Auto accident: record driver, vehicle, location, police and medical facts, business use, policy dates, liability limits, collision deductible, rental need, and possible UM/UIM. Rental car: check vehicle type, rental agreement, territory, business purpose, loss-of-use demand, credit card benefits, and the insured's actual auto form.

For every scenario, create a two-part file note: confirmed facts and unanswered coverage questions. The insurer makes the claim decision; the agent can make the notice complete and keep the client informed.

Field exercise. Choose two scenarios and complete the claims logic checklist in the workbook.

sections.title: Chapter 19 Commercial Lines Scenarios
sections.html:
Chapter 19 Commercial Lines Scenarios

Contractor damages a client's property: distinguish property being worked on from separate surrounding property; identify subcontractors, contracts, completed or ongoing operations, and CGL exclusions. Business interruption: verify direct physical loss or another endorsed trigger, lost revenue calculation, continuing expenses, waiting period, and the restoration timeline.

Slip and fall: identify location, control of premises, claimant status, alleged condition, injuries, video, witnesses, CGL period and insured parties. Cyber breach: preserve devices and logs, notify the insurer's response team, check ransomware, privacy, business interruption, social engineering and vendor sublimits. Employee injury: establish employment facts and workers compensation status; do not assume the CGL substitutes for employers liability.

The practical skill is to separate an event into parallel coverage questions. A café fire can create property damage, spoiled stock, business income loss, employee injury, and liability to a neighboring tenant. Each may call for a different policy and adjuster.

Field exercise. Create one combined loss timeline for the café fire with a separate notification path for each potentially involved policy.

sections.title: Chapter 20 Claims Walkthroughs
sections.html:
Chapter 20 Claims Walkthroughs

A claim begins with reported facts, not a confirmed coverage decision. First address safety and reasonable mitigation. Record the date, place, cause as reported, parties, damaged property, and immediate needs. Send notice according to carrier procedures and preserve confirmation. Then identify the policy period, coverage part, form, endorsements, limits, deductible and loss evidence.

The investigation may include statements, inspection, expert reports, causation analysis, estimates, medical records, police reports, contracts, and financial records. The adjuster may reserve rights, seek more information, accept in whole or part, or deny with reasons. Coverage, liability, and valuation are separate questions. A denial can result from no coverage grant, an exclusion, unmet conditions, lack of proof, exhausted limits, or a policy outside the relevant period.

When settlement is proposed, verify how deductible, depreciation, salvage, subrogation, other insurance, and payment recipients are handled. An agent should clarify process and direct disputes to the claims manager or formal review channel. A chronological, factual file note protects the client and agency.

Field exercise. Write a claim triage memo for a two-day café closure caused by an off-premises utility outage.

sections.title: Bonus Texas Agent Modules
sections.html:
Bonus Texas Agent Modules

Chapter 21 TWIA FAIR Plans and Coastal Risks

TWIA offers wind and hail coverage for eligible properties in designated Texas coastal areas when coverage is not available in the private market under its rules. The Texas FAIR Plan Association is a residual market option for eligible Texas properties denied by standard carriers. They serve different needs and have distinct eligibility, forms, limits, deductibles, and application processes.

A coastal household may need a homeowners policy, a separate TWIA wind and hail policy, and flood coverage. Map which event belongs to each policy, confirm all effective dates, and inspect the actual exclusions. A hurricane can create wind and flood damage that require separate investigation. Flood coverage can have a waiting period with exceptions; do not wait for a named storm to discuss it.

Before presenting a quote, check the association's current eligibility rules, required declinations, location, property condition, and agent registration. Explain that residual market availability does not guarantee identical protection to a preferred homeowners contract.

Field exercise. Prepare a three-policy coverage map for a home near the coast.

sections.title: Chapter 22 Texas Non Subscriber Workers Compensation
sections.html:
Chapter 22 Texas Non Subscriber Workers Compensation

Texas private employers generally may elect not to subscribe to workers compensation, subject to important exceptions. Nonsubscription is an operational and legal decision, not a mere premium comparison. TDI's Division of Workers Compensation describes notice and reporting requirements for employers without coverage or that end coverage. An alternative benefit plan does not automatically recreate the statutory workers compensation system.

For the insurance review, map employee injuries, occupational accidents, third-party suits, contractual requirements, employers liability availability, and any occupational accident or employer liability product. A producer should bring in qualified workers compensation, benefits, and legal specialists when the client asks about the consequences of nonsubscription.

Document the employer's actual coverage status and requested review. Never describe a nonsubscriber plan as 'workers compensation' unless it is truly that coverage.

Field exercise. Draft a referral note for a ten-person contractor considering nonsubscription.

sections.title: Chapter 23 Texas Specific Endorsements and Forms
sections.html:
Chapter 23 Texas Specific Endorsements and Forms

Texas coverage analysis requires reading the issued carrier's forms. A familiar national form label may conceal a Texas-specific amendment or a company-specific contract. Build a form schedule for each account: base policy, state amendatory endorsement, roof or wind terms, water and foundation terms, vacancy or occupancy provisions, liability amendments, and any exclusion added at renewal.

For personal lines, compare roof ACV, cosmetic hail, water backup, foundation, flood, wind/hail, rental use, and umbrella underlying requirements. For commercial lines, compare additional insured, waiver of subrogation, primary and noncontributory, protective safeguards, business income, ordinance or law, and equipment breakdown endorsements. The title alone does not tell you the operative language.

A practical form audit asks: What changed from last year? What did this endorsement delete, replace, or add? Which exposure is affected? Which limit, sublimit, deductible, or condition applies? What must the client do? Put the answer into a short, accurate renewal note and save the actual pages.

Field exercise. Review an expiring and renewal package with one new water exclusion and write a client notice.

sections.title: Workbook and sixteen week course
sections.html:
Workbook and sixteen week course

Learning outcomes

Explain personal auto, homeowners, dwelling, flood, umbrella, commercial property, general liability, business auto, workers compensation, and common specialty exposures in client language.

Build a documented exposure map and distinguish what the client requested from what the risk requires.

Read insuring agreements, definitions, exclusions, exceptions, conditions, endorsements, limits, and valuation provisions in the correct order.

Compare quotations on coverage and contract terms before comparing premiums.

Make underwriting submissions that are complete and truthful; identify referral, inspection, eligibility, and binding issues.

Triage a claim by preserving facts, finding possible coverage paths, identifying deadlines, and referring the decision to the insurer.

Use Texas regulator resources, carrier procedures, and supervisor review for compliance decisions; maintain a current CE and license record.

sections.title: How to use the program
sections.html:
How to use the program

Weekly rhythm

What to do

Day 1

Read the assigned official guide and a current carrier form or manual.

Day 2

Annotate a policy: coverage trigger, definitions, exclusions, conditions, limits, endorsements.

Day 3

Work the scenario and draft a client explanation of 150 to 250 words.

Day 4

Review with an experienced P&C producer or carrier trainer; correct the file.

Day 5

Score the deliverable and log unresolved questions for follow up.

Evidence portfolio. Save a coverage comparison, exposure worksheet, annotated forms, underwriting memo, claim triage note, and client communication for each relevant week. Remove names, addresses, policy numbers, and health or financial details from training copies.

sections.title: Sixteen week learning plan
sections.html:
Sixteen week learning plan

Week 1 Agency workflow and professional judgment

Study and practice. Map the client journey from prospect to renewal. Read license status, appointment, authority, E&O, premium handling, file notes, and escalation procedures with your agency.

Deliverable. Build a one page transaction checklist and identify who may quote, bind, issue, endorse, and handle claims.

Week 2 Policy anatomy and interpretation

Study and practice. Read a specimen declarations page, base form, schedule, and three endorsements. Practice finding the grant of coverage before exclusions and exceptions.

Deliverable. Create a form inventory and annotate two coverage questions with page and clause references.

Week 3 Personal auto foundations

Study and practice. Liability, defense, permissive use, UM/UIM, PIP, medical payments, collision, comprehensive, rental and towing; examine drivers, garaging, business use, and vehicles.

Deliverable. Compare a Texas minimum limits quote with a stronger limits quote; explain the uninsured loss possibilities.

Week 4 Auto edge cases and claims

Study and practice. Rideshare, delivery, household drivers, nonowned and rental vehicles, loan or lease, total loss, and comparative liability; carrier form specifics control.

Deliverable. Complete Auto case A and a claim timeline with facts still needed.

Week 5 Homeowners structure and valuation

Study and practice. Coverage A to F, other structures, contents, loss of use, liability, replacement cost, actual cash value, roof settlements, deductibles, and coinsurance concepts.

Deliverable. Compare two homeowners offers using a coverage matrix and replacement cost discussion.

Week 6 Home endorsements and catastrophe gaps

Study and practice. Water backup, seepage, foundation, equipment breakdown, service line, scheduled valuables, flood, wind and hail, TWIA eligibility, and umbrella attachment.

Deliverable. Complete Home case B and a separate flood and wind discussion for a coastal and inland home.

Week 7 Personal umbrella and household account

Study and practice. Underlying limits, retained limit, exclusions, defense, autos, rentals, pools, vacant property, and potential gaps between primary and umbrella forms.

Deliverable. Write a household exposure interview and an umbrella referral memo.

Week 8 Texas personal lines checkpoint

Study and practice. Texas Consumer Bill of Rights, disclosures, quotes, advertising, documentation, cancellation and nonrenewal questions, complaint escalation, CE ledger.

Deliverable. Do a 30 minute observed household review; reach 80 percent on the first checkpoint.

Week 9 Commercial discovery and account design

Study and practice. Entity, premises, operations, payroll, sales, subcontractors, property schedule, contracts, loss history, certificates, and renewal dates.

Deliverable. Create a small business exposure map and submission checklist.

Week 10 Commercial property and business income

Study and practice. Building versus business personal property; causes of loss, valuation, coinsurance, vacancy, ordinance or law, equipment breakdown, business income and extra expense.

Deliverable. Model a property loss with a waiting period, period of restoration, and missing documentation.

Week 11 Commercial general liability and contracts

Study and practice. Occurrence trigger, bodily injury/property damage, personal and advertising injury, products and completed operations, additional insured status, contractual liability, and exclusions.

Deliverable. Annotate a CGL coverage path and review a sample lease request without promising contract compliance.

Week 12 Business auto and workers compensation

Study and practice. Owned, hired, and nonowned autos; symbols and driver schedules; employee injuries, Texas subscriber versus nonsubscriber considerations, employers liability, and payroll classification.

Deliverable. Build an auto and worker exposure map for a contractor; list underwriting referrals.

Week 13 BOP, specialty and market placement

Study and practice. BOP eligibility, professional liability versus CGL, cyber, inland marine, builders risk, excess and surplus lines; identify who is authorized to place each risk.

Deliverable. Write a two market placement memo that compares exclusions, retentions, limits, and financial terms.

Week 14 Underwriting lab

Study and practice. Appetite, hazards, protective safeguards, construction, occupancy, location, loss runs, inspections, risk controls, and adverse action follow up.

Deliverable. Submit two complete fictional applications and a referral memo; correct all material omissions.

Week 15 Claims and renewal lab

Study and practice. First notice of loss, evidence preservation, mitigation, insurer communications, reserving uncertainty, subrogation, salvage, renewal changes and remarketing.

Deliverable. Complete three claim triages and a 90 day renewal calendar.

Week 16 Capstone and supervised review

Study and practice. Handle one household and one small business from discovery through coverage comparison, recommendation, underwriting, claims question and compliance audit.

Deliverable. Present both files to a mentor using the rubric; remediate each critical miss and repeat.

sections.title: Policy interpretation method
sections.html:
Policy interpretation method

1. Fix the facts: named insured, property or person, place, event, date, activity, and claimed damage. Separate confirmed from assumed facts.

2. Identify the policy period, coverage part, declarations, schedules, form edition, and every relevant endorsement.

3. Find the insuring agreement or coverage grant and test every element of its trigger.

4. Read definitions and who or what is an insured or covered property.

5. Read exclusions, exceptions, and endorsements that amend the base form. An endorsement may broaden or narrow coverage.

6. Apply conditions, duties after loss, reporting, notice, protective safeguards, and any other prerequisites.

7. Apply limits, sublimits, deductibles, valuation, coinsurance, and other insurance provisions.

8. Write a provisional explanation: likely path, clause citations, missing facts, potential limits, and what the insurer must decide.

sections.title: Illustrative policy wording drills
sections.html:
Illustrative policy wording drills

The following excerpts are invented for training. They are deliberately incomplete. For each, answer: Which clause matters, what facts are missing, what could change the result, and how would you explain the uncertainty?

P1 Home water

Training excerpt. We cover sudden and accidental discharge of water from plumbing. We do not cover continuous or repeated seepage occurring over weeks, months, or years.

Facts. A pipe behind a wall leaks. Staining appeared two months ago; the homeowner noticed a sudden ceiling collapse today.

Review points. Distinguish sudden collapse from duration of leakage. Seek plumber findings, photographs, dates, and any endorsement. Do not infer the cause or promise payment.

P2 Home roof

Training excerpt. Roof loss is settled at actual cash value unless the schedule states replacement cost. Wind and hail deductible is 2 percent of Coverage A.

Facts. Coverage A is $400,000; a wind loss is reported with a $12,000 replacement estimate.

Review points. Calculate the illustrative deductible as $8,000, but depreciation and covered scope remain unknown. Verify schedule and whether a roof endorsement changes settlement.

P3 Auto delivery

Training excerpt. Liability coverage does not apply while the insured auto is being used to carry property for a fee, except a use specifically restored by endorsement.

Facts. A client makes restaurant deliveries on weekends and has a collision after accepting an order.

Review points. Identify policy version, delivery stage, applicable endorsement, collision terms, and any platform insurance. Refer to carrier before asserting coverage.

P4 Commercial property vacancy

Training excerpt. Loss by vandalism is excluded if the building has been vacant for more than 60 consecutive days before loss, unless a vacancy permit applies.

Facts. A retail tenant moved out 70 days ago; the owner reports broken windows.

Review points. Determine vacancy definition, percentage of occupancy, who owns insured interest, loss date, permits, and other damage. Do not substitute an ordinary meaning of vacancy.

P5 CGL completed work

Training excerpt. The policy covers bodily injury caused by an occurrence during the policy period, subject to all exclusions. Products completed operations aggregate applies as stated in declarations.

Facts. A contractor finished a railing last year. It fails and injures a visitor this year.

Review points. Check occurrence timing, policy year, named insured, scope of work, alleged defect, exclusions, aggregate, and other insurance; insurer decides defense and indemnity.

P6 Business income

Training excerpt. Covered business income loss must result from necessary suspension caused by direct physical loss to property at the premises from a covered cause of loss.

Facts. A power outage closes a café for two days without reported physical damage at the premises.

Review points. Test direct physical loss, covered cause, utility services endorsement, waiting period, records, and extra expense; lost revenue alone does not establish the stated trigger.

sections.title: Case files and scenario assignments
sections.html:
Case files and scenario assignments

A Texas family auto

Client facts. Two adults, a 19 year old resident child, a financed SUV, a second older car, and occasional food delivery. Existing limits are 30/60/25.

Assignment. Interview drivers and use; compare 30/60/25 with higher liability, UM/UIM, PIP, collision, comprehensive, rental, and umbrella eligibility. Explain what is contingent on carrier forms.

B Home sale and hail

Client facts. A Dallas buyer is closing in 21 days. A roof has prior hail repairs. Quotes have different roof settlement terms and 1 percent versus 2 percent wind/hail deductibles.

Assignment. Build a same basis comparison; calculate deductibles from each Coverage A amount; ask about inspection, prior claims, binder timing, mortgage requirements, and flood separately.

C Gulf Coast relocation

Client facts. A family is buying near the coast, assumes the homeowners policy covers all wind and rising water, and wants immediate coverage.

Assignment. Map homeowners, possible TWIA wind and hail, and flood placements; verify eligibility and effective dates. Explain why agent must confirm each policy and waiting period.

D Main Street café

Client facts. A café leases space, has $180,000 equipment and improvements, six workers, delivery activity, customer foot traffic, and seasonal revenue.

Assignment. Build property, business income, CGL, products, hired/nonowned or owned auto, workers compensation decision, cyber and equipment breakdown discussion.

E Small contractor

Client facts. A renovation contractor uses two trucks and subcontractors, stores tools at jobsites, and signs a lease requiring an additional insured endorsement.

Assignment. Separate CGL from professional advice and faulty workmanship, compare business auto and inland marine, collect subcontractor certificates, review contract with agency counsel or supervisor.

F Rental portfolio

Client facts. A real estate investor has three rentals, one vacant for renovation, and a short term rental under consideration.

Assignment. Identify occupancy, dwelling and liability forms, vacancy and rental endorsements, building values, flood, wind, and umbrella schedule; obtain carrier approval before binding.

G Cyber event

Client facts. A bookkeeper's laptop is stolen with client tax files, and a vendor demands reimbursement.

Assignment. Distinguish first party response and third party liability; gather privacy and breach facts, policy dates, retroactive date if applicable, vendor contract, and breach coach procedure.

H Renewal shock

Client facts. A homeowner's premium rises 35 percent and the renewal changes roof settlement and deductible.

Assignment. Prepare change summary, compare alternative quotes on equal terms, document client choice, and avoid switching before effective dates are confirmed.

sections.title: Claims logic training
sections.html:
Claims logic training

Use this sequence on every claim scenario: safety and mitigation; notice and timestamps; policy and form identification; loss mechanism; potential coverage trigger; exclusions and exceptions; duties and evidence; deductible and valuation; insurer decision; client update and file note. Record what is unknown.

Claim

Questions to investigate

Agent output

Burst pipe

When did damage begin? What failed? Is damage sudden or repeated? Is mold alleged? Who inspected it?

Neutral first notice, mitigation advice consistent with policy, evidence list.

Hail roof

Date and location? Roof age? Prior damage? Wind/hail deductible? ACV or replacement?

Coverage question list and deductible illustration, with insurer referral.

Rear end collision

Drivers, police report, injuries, vehicle use, permissive use, UM/UIM, rental need?

Timeline, coverages to ask adjuster about, no fault or payment promise.

Business fire

Direct damage? Closure order? Waiting period? Revenue and payroll records? Alternate location?

Property and business income document request list.

Injured subcontractor

Employer status, contract, site control, certificates, CGL and workers compensation facts?

Separate notices to potentially involved carriers; preserve contract and status facts.

Flood after storm

Where did water originate? Surface water or roof opening? Wind and flood policies effective?

Separate cause of loss questions and reports to appropriate insurers.

sections.title: Underwriting reasoning lab
sections.html:
Underwriting reasoning lab

For each risk, write four fields: material fact, why an underwriter cares, evidence to request, and permissible next step. Never conceal an adverse fact or alter an application to fit appetite.

A home has a 25 year old roof and two recent water claims. Explain roof condition, frequency, inspection and mitigation questions; seek carrier underwriting review.

A family says a resident teenager rarely drives. Explain household driver disclosure and permissive use questions; record the carrier's written rules.

A small business reports $500,000 sales but payment records suggest $900,000. Reconcile gross sales before submission.

A contractor uses subcontractors for 70 percent of work. Request contracts, scope, certificates and payroll or cost split; ask carrier how the classification applies.

A coastal property has an elevated foundation and prior flood claim. Verify location, construction, flood loss history, elevation information and market eligibility.

A restaurant adds alcohol service and delivery midterm. Identify changed hazard and effective date; submit endorsement or market referral promptly.

A vacant building has temporary renovations. Ask about vacancy definition, security, permits, construction timetable and protective safeguards.

A client demands immediate coverage on a Friday evening. Identify actual binding authority and required payment or inspection conditions; provide no verbal binder without authority.

sections.title: Texas compliance modules
sections.html:
Texas compliance modules

Licensing and authority

Verify active license, agency affiliation and carrier appointment or binding authority before transacting. Review agency procedures for premium handling, records and E&O. TDI says insurer appointments must be filed before agent transactions. Source to check: TDI licensing and appointment pages.

Continuing education

For a Texas General Lines P&C license, TDI lists 24 hours every two years including 3 hours of ethics. Track your own renewal and CE transcript; confirm any exceptions with TDI. Source to check: TDI P&C license management and CE pages.

Consumer communication

Use TDI's auto and home Consumer Bill of Rights and comparison worksheets. Do not equate a quote with a binder or imply all named perils are covered. Source to check: TDI consumer guides.

Texas personal lines exposures

Know the 30/60/25 auto liability minimum but demonstrate why a client may choose higher limits. Explain that standard home coverage generally excludes flood; review coastal wind/hail separately. Source to check: TDI auto and home guides.

Business and workers compensation

Review commercial policy rights and notice rules by line. Texas private employers generally may choose whether to carry workers compensation, with exceptions; refer status and notice questions to current DWC guidance. Source to check: TDI commercial rights and DWC.

Claims and complaints

Help submit complete facts and preserve records; avoid assigning fault, interpreting a live claim as final, or committing the insurer to payment. Route disputed decisions through insurer and TDI complaint channels. Source to check: TDI claims and consumer resources.

Advertising and referral practices

Have the agency compliance lead review websites, testimonials, gifts, referral fees, rebating, and co-marketing before launch, especially when real estate leads and insurance leads overlap. Source to check: TDI and agency counsel.

Data and confidentiality

Use approved CRM, access controls and secure file exchange for applications, driver details and claim records. Test breach escalation with the agency's actual procedures. Source to check: Agency privacy and security procedures.

sections.title: Assessments and scoring
sections.html:
Assessments and scoring

Measure

Points

Passing evidence

Exposure discovery

20

Material exposures identified; unknowns and client priorities recorded.

Policy interpretation

25

Correct form path, clause citations, endorsements, limits and uncertainty.

Coverage comparison

15

Equal basis comparisons and clear tradeoffs, without premium only ranking.

Underwriting quality

15

Complete truthful submission, referral and binding authority.

Claims logic

15

Neutral facts, evidence, mitigation, insurer escalation and dates.

Texas compliance and communication

10

Current source verification, file notes, appropriate client wording.

Pass standard. Score at least 85 of 100 on the week 16 capstone, at least 80 on each of the two case files, and zero critical misses. A critical miss is a fabricated coverage promise, concealed material fact, unauthorized binder, omitted major exclusion after discovery, or mishandled private client data. Rewrite and re-present any critical miss.

Portfolio check. A mentor should be able to reconstruct your reasoning from the facts, policy forms, quote versions, questions asked, recommendation, client response, and follow up dates.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.html:
Glossary

Actual cash value. A loss settlement measure commonly reflecting replacement cost less depreciation, subject to the policy.

Additional insured. A party granted specified liability protection by an actual endorsement, within its terms.

Aggregate limit. The most an insurer will pay for a defined category of claims during the policy period.

Binder. Temporary evidence of coverage issued only with valid authority and required conditions.

Business income. Coverage for defined income loss after a qualifying suspension and covered cause, subject to form terms.

Coinsurance. A property condition that can reduce partial loss payment if the insured carries less than the required amount.

Declarations. Policy pages identifying the insured, period, coverages, limits, deductibles and scheduled exposures.

Deductible. The portion of an otherwise covered loss borne by the insured under the policy calculation.

Endorsement. A form that adds, removes, or changes policy wording.

Exclusion. A provision that removes otherwise potentially applicable coverage for specified circumstances.

Hired auto. An auto leased, hired, rented or borrowed within the applicable business auto definition.

Insuring agreement. The clause stating the insurer's coverage promise and the elements of its trigger.

Loss runs. Insurer or agency record of a risk's reported losses during a period.

Nonowned auto. An auto used in a business but not owned, leased, hired, rented or borrowed by it, under the applicable form.

Occurrence. An event or continuous exposure defined by the policy; its meaning matters for liability timing.

Period of restoration. The defined time used in business income coverage to measure interruption after covered damage.

Replacement cost. A settlement basis tied to replacing covered property under the policy's terms, often subject to conditions.

Retained limit. The amount an insured may have to bear before certain umbrella coverage responds.

Subrogation. An insurer's pursuit of recovery from a responsible party after paying a covered loss.

Sublimit. A lower cap applying to a specified kind of property, loss, or expense.

Underwriting appetite. A carrier's current criteria for risks it is willing to consider and on what terms.

Vacancy. A policy-defined condition concerning occupancy or use, potentially affecting coverage.

Texas Supreme Court case reference: USAA Texas Lloyds Co. v. Menchaca, corrected opinion, https://www.txcourts.gov/media/1441365/140721.pdf
